cls: Ethanol - topical antiseptic / pharmaceutical solvent; injectable neurolytic and antidote agent
pharm: Ethyl alcohol (ethanol) used in medicine as a topical antiseptic and disinfectant (commonly 60-90% solutions), as a pharmaceutical solvent and preservative, as dehydrated (anhydrous) alcohol for injection used as a neurolytic agent and for tissue ablation/embolization, and historically as an intravenous antidote for methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning by competing for alcohol dehydrogenase.
quick: Topical: 60-90% to skin before procedures; injectable use is procedure-specific
Topical safe; avoid systemic/ingested ethanol exposure
Caution with systemic ethanol (e.g., antidote infusions)
Avoid systemic ethanol in liver disease
Itself is alcohol - additive CNS depression if ingested with depressants
Local skin integrity; for systemic use: CNS status, blood ethanol/glucose
summary: In medicine 'alcohol' refers to ethanol (ethyl alcohol). Its principal medicinal uses are topical: as a skin antiseptic and disinfectant (60-90% solutions, including in hand sanitizers and pre-injection skin preparation) and as a solvent/preservative in many formulations. Dehydrated (anhydrous, >=98%) alcohol is a prescription injectable used as a neurolytic agent for chronic pain (e.g., celiac plexus or trigeminal nerve block), for therapeutic ablation/embolization, and for percutaneous tumor ablation. Intravenous/oral ethanol has historically been used as an antidote in methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning by competing for the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase (now largely replaced by fomepizole). Topical ethanol is for external use only, is highly flammable, and must be kept from eyes and broken skin; systemic ethanol causes dose-dependent central nervous system depression and organ toxicity.
indications: Topical antiseptic and skin disinfection (e.g., pre-injection/pre-procedure skin prep, hand hygiene)
Pharmaceutical solvent, vehicle, and preservative in liquid formulations
Dehydrated alcohol injection as a neurolytic agent for intractable chronic pain (e.g., celiac plexus block, trigeminal neuralgia)
Dehydrated alcohol for percutaneous/transcatheter tissue ablation or embolization (e.g., tumors, vascular malformations)
Antidote for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning (competitive inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase) where fomepizole is unavailable

dosage.d: Apply 60-90% ethanol solution to clean skin and allow to dry before the procedure
dosage.t: As needed before procedures / hand hygiene
dosage.n: External use only; do not apply to broken skin or mucosa

dosage.d: Dehydrated alcohol (>=98%) in small volumes titrated to the target nerve/plexus by the proceduralist
dosage.n: Specialist procedure; volume depends on the target

dosage.d: Dehydrated alcohol volume individualized to lesion size and site by the operator
dosage.n: Limit total volume to avoid systemic intoxication

dosage.d: Loading then maintenance infusion titrated to a blood ethanol of ~100-150 mg/dL
dosage.n: Fomepizole is now preferred; requires intensive monitoring

admin: Topical: apply to intact skin and allow to dry; keep away from eyes, mucous membranes, and open wounds; do not use near open flame, sparks, or while smoking (highly flammable)
Allow alcohol-based skin prep to dry fully before electrosurgery or draping to avoid fire
Dehydrated alcohol injections for neurolysis or ablation are performed only by trained specialists, usually under imaging guidance, with strict attention to placement and total volume
For antidote use, administer ethanol by a controlled route with frequent monitoring of blood ethanol, glucose, and the patient's neurologic status
Do not inject topical/disinfectant alcohol or administer it for ingestion; never use methylated/denatured spirit for any internal or injectable purpose
moa: Ethanol exerts different actions depending on use. As a topical antiseptic, it denatures and coagulates microbial proteins and disrupts lipid membranes, killing bacteria, many viruses, and fungi; this requires water (hence 60-90% rather than 100% is most effective). As a neurolytic and ablative agent, injected dehydrated alcohol causes dehydration, protein precipitation, and chemical destruction of nerve tissue or other cells, producing nerve block or tissue necrosis. As an antidote for methanol/ethylene glycol poisoning, ethanol competitively binds alcohol dehydrogenase with higher affinity than the toxic alcohols, preventing their metabolism to toxic aldehydes/acids and allowing safe elimination. Systemically, ethanol is a CNS depressant that potentiates GABA-A receptor activity and inhibits NMDA glutamate receptors, producing dose-dependent sedation and intoxication.

absolute: Application to or near the eyes, mucous membranes, or open/broken skin (topical antiseptic)
Use near open flame, electrocautery before drying, or other ignition sources (flammability)
Neurolytic/ablative injection at sites where spread would damage vital structures (relative to procedure)
relative: Systemic ethanol in patients with active liver disease, pancreatitis, or alcohol use disorder
Pregnancy and lactation for systemic/ingested ethanol
Concurrent CNS depressants (additive effect with systemic ethanol)
Disulfiram or metronidazole therapy (disulfiram-like reaction with systemic ethanol)
monitor: Local skin integrity and absence of irritation (topical)
For systemic/antidote use: blood ethanol, blood glucose, electrolytes, and neurologic status
Procedure-related complications for neurolysis/ablation (e.g., neuritis, tissue injury)

preg: Topical ethanol antiseptic use is considered safe in pregnancy. Systemic exposure to ethanol (ingestion) is harmful and can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders - there is no known safe amount of alcohol in pregnancy, so ingested/systemic ethanol should be avoided.
lact: Topical antiseptic use is compatible with breastfeeding. Systemic/ingested ethanol passes into breast milk and can affect the infant and milk production; avoid alcohol ingestion during breastfeeding or time feeds well away from any intake.
renal: Topical use needs no adjustment. For systemic ethanol (e.g., antidote infusions), renal function affects fluid/electrolyte handling and toxic-alcohol clearance; use with caution and close monitoring, and recognize that hemodialysis removes both ethanol and the toxic alcohols.
hepatic: Topical use needs no adjustment. Systemic ethanol is metabolized hepatically and is contraindicated or used only with great caution in significant liver disease; impaired hepatic function reduces clearance and increases toxicity.

major: CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, barbiturates, antipsychotics, sedating antihistamines) - additive central nervous system and respiratory depression with systemic ethanol
Disulfiram - severe disulfiram-ethanol reaction (flushing, vomiting, hypotension) with systemic ethanol
moderate: Metronidazole, tinidazole, and some cephalosporins - possible disulfiram-like reaction with ingested ethanol
Insulin and sulfonylureas - increased hypoglycemia risk with systemic ethanol
Hepatotoxic drugs (e.g., paracetamol/acetaminophen in chronic heavy use) - increased liver injury
minor: Topical alcohol has no clinically significant systemic interactions
interactions.food: Not applicable to medicinal/topical use; with ingestion, food slows ethanol absorption.
interactions.alcohol: This agent IS alcohol - additional ingested alcohol simply increases systemic ethanol effects and toxicity.
interactions.diagnostics: Systemic ethanol can cause hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis (in toxic-alcohol poisoning context), and is itself measured as blood alcohol; topical use may interfere with some skin tests at the application site.

common: Local skin dryness, irritation, or stinging (topical)
Transient burning on application to abraded skin
serious: Chemical/thermal burns and fires from ignition of alcohol-based preparations
Systemic intoxication, CNS and respiratory depression with significant systemic exposure
Neuritis or unintended tissue damage after neurolytic/ablation injection
Inadvertent intoxication in infants from excessive topical use on large/occluded areas
rare: Methemoglobinemia or severe local reactions (formulation dependent)
Cardiac arrhythmia with high systemic levels
emergency: Fire/burn during a procedure using alcohol skin prep
Severe ethanol intoxication with coma or respiratory depression
Hypoglycemia or profound metabolic disturbance from systemic ethanol

monitoring: Local skin condition and complete drying before procedures (fire safety)
Signs of systemic absorption/intoxication, especially in infants or with large occluded areas
For systemic/antidote use: blood ethanol level, blood glucose, electrolytes, acid-base status, and neurologic/respiratory status
Procedure site for complications after neurolytic or ablative injection
counsel: Use alcohol antiseptic on the skin only - keep it away from your eyes, mouth, and any cuts or wounds
Alcohol is highly flammable - let it dry completely and keep it away from flames, sparks, and cigarettes
Do not drink any alcohol-based antiseptic, hand sanitizer, or methylated spirit - it can be poisonous
Frequent use can dry your skin; use a moisturizer if needed
If you have a nerve block or tissue treatment with alcohol, follow your specialist's after-care instructions
Avoid drinking alcohol if you take medicines like metronidazole or disulfiram, or sedatives, because of dangerous reactions
pk: Topical antiseptic action within seconds to minutes; systemic CNS effects within minutes of ingestion
Blood ethanol peaks ~30-90 minutes after ingestion
Eliminated by zero-order kinetics (~15-20 mg/dL per hour), not a fixed half-life
Topical effect lasts while wet/until dry; systemic effects depend on dose
Store in a tightly closed container away from heat and open flame (highly flammable)
pearls: 'Alcohol' in pharmacy means ethanol; the common medicinal role is a topical antiseptic at 60-90% (needs some water to be most effective)
Highly flammable - allow alcohol skin preps to dry fully before electrosurgery/draping to prevent surgical fires
Dehydrated (anhydrous) alcohol injection is a specialist neurolytic/ablative agent (e.g., celiac plexus block, tumor ablation) - limit volume to avoid systemic intoxication
As a toxic-alcohol antidote it competes for alcohol dehydrogenase against methanol/ethylene glycol, but fomepizole is now preferred
Never ingest antiseptic, sanitizer, or denatured/methylated spirit; systemic ethanol is a CNS depressant with additive sedation and disulfiram-like interactions
No safe amount of ingested alcohol in pregnancy; topical antiseptic use, however, is considered safe
missed: Medicinal alcohol is used as needed (topical antiseptic) or as a clinician-administered procedure/antidote, so there is no routine dosing schedule or missed-dose scenario for patients.
overdose: Topical overuse can cause skin irritation and, rarely, systemic absorption (especially in infants). Systemic ethanol overdose (excessive injection volume or ingestion) causes CNS depression, ataxia, vomiting, hypoglycemia, respiratory depression, coma, and potentially death. There is no specific reversal agent; management is supportive with airway/breathing/circulation support, correction of hypoglycemia and electrolytes, and, in severe poisoning, hemodialysis to remove ethanol (and any co-ingested toxic alcohols).
